items.title: Product Managers Are Thriving in the AI Era
points: Open PM roles grew 56% since early 2023, outpacing engineering growth of 43%.
PM hiring share increased from 16% in 2021 to 21% today, the only core tech role to gain market share.
Despite record job openings, actual hiring for all core roles remained flat or declined, signaling that landing top talent has become harder even as demand rises.
PM roles hit a 4-year hiring high (up 75% from 2023 lows), even as engineering demand plateaus with just 2.5% job growth in the past year.

items.title: Engineering Growth Has Stalled
points: Engineering job openings grew just 2.5% in the past year after 29% growth through 2024, marking the first plateau in report history.
U.S. hiring for software engineers hit 113,000 in the past 12 months, down 53% from the 239,000 peak in 2022.

Forward deployed engineer roles (FDE—engineers embedded with customers to solve complex implementation problems) exploded 4.6x in the past year, reaching ~1,500 open positions, while mobile and front-end engineering demand halved.
Recruiter roles hit record highs (up nearly 300% since mid-2023), potentially signaling a future engineering hiring reacceleration.

items.title: Design Roles Collapse to Historic Lows
points: Just 1,900 product design roles are open globally, down 28% year-over-year and the lowest on record.
U.S. companies hired only 12,600 product designers in the past 12 months, less than half the 27,600 hired in 2022.
The ratio of PM roles to design roles hit 3.8:1, up from 2.6 earlier this year and 1.9 in early 2023.
User research experienced the steepest collapse of any role with hiring down 66% since 2022 (5,300 to 1,800 hires), with just 108 open UXR positions globally.

items.title: AI Skills Now Define Tech Job Markets Across All Roles
points: LLM (large language model, an AI system trained on vast amounts of text to generate human-like responses) is the #1 mentioned skill in PM job descriptions, replacing SQL, Jira, and AWS.
Claude (Anthropic's AI assistant) is the #3 most-mentioned skill for PMs and #2 for designers, with Cursor and OpenAI also in top eight PM skills.
For engineers, Python remains dominant but LLM just surpassed Java in job postings, while Java demand fell sharply over the past year.
Figma demand among designers continues growing despite the company's stock decline, but Claude and Cursor have now edged past CSS in job description frequency.

items.title: Tech Jobs Concentrate in Bay Area While Remote Plummets
points: Bay Area tech job openings surged 43% in the past year and now represent 15% of all global roles, a record high.
One in four open PM and design roles is Bay Area-based, and one in five engineering roles, all at record highs and nearly doubled since 2022.
Remote roles fell to 14% of all tech positions, down from 21% in late 2022; remote engineering roles dropped from 25% to 14%.
For the first time, there are now more open PM/engineering/design roles in the Bay Area than remote roles globally, a complete reversal from four years ago.

items.title: Anthropic Releases Claude Fable 5.2: Powerful but Underwhelming for Everyday Use
points: Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.2 is its most powerful model yet, leading all benchmarks by significant margins, but users struggle to find practical reasons to switch from the cheaper, faster Opus 5.5 for everyday tasks.

Fable 5.2 excels at ambitious, long-running projects: it coordinated 1,000+ AI agents to build a bootable operating system, solved open physics problems, and formalized Fermat's Last Theorem in machine-readable code.

The model costs 20% less per token but remains extremely expensive for complex tasks (up to $26.54 per request on maximum effort), and is slower, pickier, and less versatile than predecessors outside its specialized strengths.

Early adopters built production-grade tools—a video editor, water safety maps, game engines—that weren't feasible before, suggesting it unlocks new capabilities rather than just incremental improvements.

The model exhibits 'jagged AGI': it handles research, coding, and creative projects at near-expert levels but lacks human judgment about quality, often producing work that's accurate but too long, repetitive, or missing the point.

items.title: Benchmark Performance: Dominant but Uneven
points: Fable 5.2 leads every major coding and science benchmark: 69.9% on FrontierSWE (a standardized software engineering evaluation), 4 points ahead of GPT-6 Astra; 49.1% on Frontier Code, 3.5 points ahead of Opus 5.5.
Most alarming score: Remote Labor Index (real-world freelance project completion) jumped to 41.3%, nearly doubling Opus 5.5's performance, raising concerns about AI-driven labor displacement.
Weaker on agentic knowledge work (handling complex information tasks with multiple steps), sometimes just matching Opus 5.5, suggesting the advance isn't universal.
Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index ranks Fable 5.2 at 65, but the lead shrinks dramatically on certain task types where it reverts to Opus 5.5 levels.

items.title: What It's Actually Good At: Scientific & Complex Projects
points: Solved two open problems in black hole physics by running calculations too laborious for human mathematicians.
Designed new gene therapy capsid structures, accurately predicting 28 of 34 models, accelerating biological research.
Fully formalized Fermat's Last Theorem into a machine-readable proof in 30 hours using 1,000 coordinated agents; Opus 5.5 stalled 26% through after 18 hours.

Built a bootable operating system from an empty folder with kernel drivers, file storage, login screen, and installer, demonstrating agentic coordination (directing hundreds of sub-agents autonomously) at scale.

items.title: Why Users Aren't Switching: The Friction Problem
points: Outside specialized tasks, Fable 5.2 is slower, more expensive per token ($8 input/$40 output per million vs. cheaper alternatives), and capped at half of subscriber token allowance.
Consensus from early testers: use Opus 5.5 when the goal is clear and Fable 5.2 when exploring unknowns; most daily work still favors the cheaper, faster predecessor.
Critical weakness in 'taste': the model produces technically accurate but often tedious work (overly long courses, 182-page papers) and fails to recognize when something isn't good enough.
The naming convention ('5.2' instead of '5.5') itself signals no generational leap, per critics, despite capability gains in narrow domains.

items.title: How to Actually Use It: Practical Guidance
points: Reserve for ambitious, multi-day projects where you can hand over an entire problem and let it work with minimal interruption, not piecemeal tasks.
Frame ownership clearly: tell Fable 'this codebase is yours' rather than implying it's a guest, or it acts cautiously and only reports nearby problems instead of fixing them proactively.
Ask for pushback before building: request Fable identify flaws in the idea first, then set clear approval requirements upfront.
Set effort level to 'medium' by default (Anthropic's recommendation), 'high' for everyday coding, and 'max' only for finding the ceiling of capability.

items.title: Emerging Use Cases: New Work Becomes Possible
points: Game development crossed a threshold: Fable 5.2 produces playable, fun games with polished mechanics, not just visually convincing shells.
Video production now agentic: one user built a production-quality 60-second ad in a single shot live on stream, costing $5.75 on rented GPUs.
Robotics control works without specialized training: Fable 5.2 piloted dual robotic arms on tasks it never learned, outperforming purpose-built models.
Developers built working video editors with embedded AI agents, monetizable YouTube channels, and water safety databases—projects feasible only with Fable's sustained reasoning over hours.

items.title: The Taste Problem: Excellent But Lacking Judgment
points: The model produces technically sound work but misses meta-level quality signals humans rely on: length, repetition, relevance, fun factor.
In a test, Fable 5.2 graded its own 'most impressive thing' by difficulty-to-check metrics rather than human-appreciable impact.
When asked to pitch ambitious project ideas, its first response was factually novel but irrelevant; its backup was solid but likely within Opus 5.5's capability.
Critical implication: Fable 5.2 can't reliably self-direct toward human values without explicit guidance—strong capability paired with weak judgment.

items.title: Security & Bug Hunting: Clear Winner
points: On a 105-bug planted-repository benchmark, Fable 5.2 found 58 (vs. Sonnet 5.5 Max's 51), using less than half the attempts for less money.
Real-world validation: one developer reported Fable 5.2 surfaced 10+ severe vulnerabilities that Opus 5.5 had introduced, unprompted.
Security appears to be one domain where Fable's advanced reasoning translates directly to practical advantage without the friction seen elsewhere.
